content:
I absolutely hate AI writing. And my entire job is to write about AI. So I keep a file of the new em-dash to recognize AI writing instantly:

Everyone learned the em dash trick. 
AI is trained to not write with em dashes anymore. 
Now you can get accused of using AI if you write in perfectly structured sentences.

These are some of the dead giveaways of using AI:

1. "That's not X. That's Y."
"That's not compliance. That's stalling."
Say the second half only. "They're stalling."

2. Two short bits stuck together.
"Fast. Simple." "No fluff. Just answers."
Pick only one to write like a real person.

3. "Less a hammer, more a scalpel."
Visualizing two pictures with no advice. Directly say what to do instead.

4. Clapping for itself.
"And that matters." "That's the part everyone misses." "Which is exactly the point."
Delete them all. You lose nothing. I promise.

5. "It's the Excel of AI agents."
Only works if I know both things. Usually I don't.

6. Warming up before talking.
"Here's the thing." "Let me be clear." "The truth is."
Start one sentence later.

7. Always three things.
"Faster, cheaper, smarter."
Real life gives you two reasons. Or five. Never always three.

8. "5 to 10 minutes."
A range means you never did it. Just say 7 minutes.

9. The ending that repeats the whole post.
"In short…" "At the end of the day…"
Just stop typing. End on a high note.

Now that you know how AI writes. Here's how to actually stop AI from doing all nine:

Step 1. Type only these two words in your prompt.
Open chat & write: "Use ASD-STE100."

That's the writing standard for plane manuals. Short words, short sentences, because a confusing sentence there can kill someone. Claude already knows it. Those words remove 80% of the bad writing. Works on ChatGPT, Gemini & Grok too.

Step 2. Get the skill so you never type it again.
I built the full version with every rule inside. It's free: https://t.co/rFXoSKBlNd

Download the zip. In Claude, click Customize on the left. Click Skills. Click Upload a skill. Drop the zip in. Type /ste to use it.

Step 3. Turn it off for fun stuff.
I asked it for a poem. Unreadable. I asked it for a LinkedIn post. It sounded German.
Use /ste for guides, steps, explanations, emails, documents. Turn it off for anything with a heart.

Step 4. Add 4 lines to your claude .md.
"follow Zinsser's four principles of quality writing: 1. Simplicity 2. Brevity 3. Clarity 4. Humanity"

/ste gives you the first three but forgets about the fourth. This prompt puts it back on the track.

Step 5. Make a forbidden .md.
Copy the 9 patterns above into a file. Tell Claude to check every draft against it.

Then add a new line every time you spot one. Your file gets better every week. Mine certainly does.

Step 6. Start a new chat more often.
If your chat is long, the writing gets worse. It repeats itself & goes back to the pretty sentences. When it feels half full, open a fresh chat & paste your files back.

The skill is free, right in your inbox: https://t.co/rFXoSKBlNd

Grok Build v1.0.4 just got a serious upgrade, giving developers more control over agent workflows with smarter follow-ups, powerful tool-input hooks, domain-controlled web search, better session tooling, and lower memory usage for finished subagents

Release Notes: v1.0.4

Features:
• New StopCancelled hook event now reports when a turn ends without completing (interrupt, permission reject, max turns, etc.).
• Recurring /loop tasks now show a one-line expiry notice in the transcript when they auto-expire after 7 days.
• Web search can now be restricted to allowed or excluded domains via [toolset.web_search] in config.toml.
• Session search index can now be disabled via GROK_SESSION_SEARCH or [features] session_search for hosts sharing $GROK_HOME.
• Drag to select and copy values on the /session-info tab; c and y shortcuts also work.
• Double-click now selects a word by default and triple-click selects the whole paragraph.
• New follow-up behavior setting lets queued messages send immediately as interjections instead of waiting for the turn to finish.
• Tool commands and MCP servers now receive a GROK_SESSION_ID environment variable matching the current session.
• Relative markdown links can now open existing files in your current working directory when no matching generated media is found.
• PreToolUse hooks can now rewrite a tool's input before it runs instead of only allowing or denying the call.

Bug Fixes:
• Queued messages no longer auto-submit while you are still editing them in the composer.
• Sessions poisoned by rejected images are now healed permanently so future turns succeed without retrying the bad image.
• Auto permission mode now correctly honors your explicit "always allow" grants and narrow allow rules from settings.
• Subagent lifecycle events are now preserved even when delivered out of order, ensuring all subagents appear correctly in the UI.
• Keystrokes typed while Grok is starting are now preserved in the composer instead of being lost.
• Background tasks killed from the UI now correctly wake the model when needed instead of staying parked after a single-task stop.
• [stop] / Ctrl+C inside a fullscreen subagent overlay now cancels the visible child session.
• Hook failures now show the first line of stderr output instead of only the exit code.
• Pasting text or dragging images while the scrollback pane is focused now focuses the composer and pastes there.
• [stop] / Ctrl+C inside a subagent drill-in view now stops the focused subagent instead of the root session.
• The dashboard shortcut now works with Ctrl+4 in terminals that do not support the Kitty keyboard protocol.
• Pasting image-only screenshots from tools like Flameshot now works on Linux without a clipboard error.
• Editing a queued prompt to a slash command like /btw now runs the command instead of sending the text to the model.
• Text typed while a plan is being generated is now preserved when the approval screen appears.
• `grok du` and worktree commands now work on Windows when only USERPROFILE is set.
• Permission-mode changes made on the welcome screen now correctly apply to the newly created session.

Performance:
• Finished subagent transcripts are now evicted from memory to reduce RAM usage and rebuilt from disk when reopened.

title:
First impressions of Grok Bot:

- With Grok Bot you don't juggle threads, you juggle named/personified agents. This seems like a ~fine mental model: hire a team of specialists that can talk among them
content:
First impressions of Grok Bot:

- With Grok Bot you don't juggle threads, you juggle named/personified agents. This seems like a ~fine mental model: hire a team of specialists that can talk among themselves to get work done.

- But this creates some problems when you want to multitask within a single agent. If you give an agent a chunky task that takes a long time, you don't really want to interrupt it or distract it mid-task. I haven't found a way to queue messages. In a thread-first world, you'd just spin up another thread.

(Technically there's a "create thread" button on each message bubble, but it feels intentionally buried and not recommended.)

- I'm biased towards using threads to create "context bubbles" for discrete tasks and prevent context contamination. But every Grok Bot agent uses a single long-running thread, and it's not obvious where discrete tasks get chunked or compacted. If I'm working with sensitive data, this forces me to create copies of the same agent so I can force context bubbles around sensitive tasks.

- I'm not sure if most people will prefer a single omni-agent that juggles threads and projects (Jarvis-style), or if people actually want to build and manage multiple discrete agents that coordinate with each other. Tradeoffs in both directions, and maybe you end up needing both models for different audiences.

- The agents themselves are capable and surprisingly dynamic. They are good at responding quickly, keeping you updated iMessage-style as they make progress on long tasks, and configuring themselves on the fly (or even reacting appropriately if you adjust their configuration manually).

- One of the surprising details that Grok Bot hides is all the thinking steps/tool calls. Almost every other AI agent exposes these, including ours at Notion. When we designed Notion Agent last year, we tried to remove these steps for the sake of simplicity, but our customers demanded we add them back both because they serve as a useful loading indicator (it's entertaining to watch computers magically do work!), and because they can be used to spot the model going off track so you can jump in and pause/steer. But I suspect model progress (speed + quality) in the last year is making both of those points less relevant, so maybe it's okay to hide more of the underlying noise from the transcript. Grok Bot agents are still good about sending mid-task progress update messages (I think this is all Grok 4.6?)

- The idea of starting a new chat with multiple agents (aka a channel? project? workspace?) is pretty nice, but agents are still a bit dumb and they go in loops talking to each other before finally shutting up. Maybe there are some prompt-fu opportunities to make them chill out.

- It's been a great experience delegating agents to work simultaneously across the cloud computer, my local machine, and Cursor cloud coding sessions. The system works really well, and I've been able to throw fun tasks at the agents without any major problems. 

- Consolidating skills, MCPs, connectors, and more complex tools behind a single "Plugins" concept feels right. It looks like everyone on the frontier is coming to the same conclusion.

- No model picker feels weird, but only because I'm used to fiddling with models/effort levels per task in all my other coding tools. Presumably Grok Bot agents are doing some routing under the hood? Making this + thinking tokens + tool calls opaque means you really have to have a "model take the wheel" mindset when using this app. Again, probably long-term right, but short-term feels uncomfortable (giving up control).

- The UI is nice. Mobile app is nice. Cursor mobile app is nice for code sessions. It just all feels...nice. Kudos to the design team for nailing the visual polish and small details. The motion design for the agent avatars is s-tier.

- Yet this shape of tool is becoming so common across so many companies (and open source!) that I don't really know how people are going to justify one $200/mo subscription vs. another. I suspect in the short term it'll come down to vibes/tribal affiliation/token subsidization, at least until there is some bigger differentiator at the capability level.

- As an experiment, I told my Grok Bot agents to switch to using a Notion database for the memory layer. They had no objections and I've watched them create ~20-30 pages in my Memory database. This feels really noisy, and I'm not sure what the impact on quality will be, but it's cool that the agents had no problem adapting to work the way I want. Whether they're actually using the database correctly under the hood, I can't tell...the whole system is quite opaque.

- Grok Bot is an odd name for an app that wants you to coordinate work across lots of bots.

- My hunch is most people don't actually have that much stuff they need to automate in their daily life. I'd love to see retention graphs!

content:
🚀 Generative AI Fundamentals

⚙️ Fine-Tuning, LoRA, PEFT, RLHF & Model Alignment

Fine-tuning and model adaptation are important topics for GenAI Engineer, LLM Engineer, and Applied AI interviews.

1. What is Fine-Tuning?

Fine-tuning is the process of taking a pretrained model and training it further on a smaller, specialized dataset.

Example:

General LLM → Financial Documents → Fine-Tuning → Financial AI Assistant

The goal is to make the model perform better on a specific task or domain.

2. Pretraining vs Fine-Tuning

Pretraining: Initial model training, Very large dataset, Learns general patterns, Expensive, Creates foundation model

Fine-Tuning: Additional training, Smaller specialized dataset, Learns specific behavior, Relatively cheaper, Adapts foundation model

Simple Example:

Pretraining: Learn general English.

Fine-tuning: Learn how to answer banking customer-support questions.

3. When Should You Fine-Tune an LLM?

Fine-tuning can be useful when you need:

✅ Consistent output format

✅ Specific writing style

✅ Domain-specific behavior

✅ Specialized classification

✅ Task-specific performance

✅ Consistent instruction following

Example: A company wants every support response to follow a specific format. Fine-tuning may be more appropriate than repeatedly putting the same style instructions into prompts.

4. When Should You NOT Fine-Tune?

Fine-tuning isn't always the best solution.

Avoid fine-tuning when the main problem is changing knowledge.

Example: A company has thousands of frequently changing policies.

Instead of continuously fine-tuning the model, use: RAG → Retrieve the latest policy → Generate answer

Rule: RAG changes the information available to the model; fine-tuning changes how the model behaves.

5. What is Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)?

PEFT allows you to adapt a large model without updating all of its parameters.

Large Frozen Model + Small Trainable Parameters → Adapted Model

Benefits: Lower GPU requirements, Lower training cost, Faster training, Smaller adaptation files

6. What is LoRA?

LoRA stands for Low-Rank Adaptation.

It is a popular PEFT technique that freezes the original model weights and adds small trainable matrices.

Original Model → Frozen + LoRA Adapters → Fine-Tuned Model

7. What are LoRA Adapters?

LoRA adapters contain the learned changes needed for a particular task.

Base Model → Finance Adapter, Medical Adapter, Coding Adapter

The same base model can therefore be adapted for different applications.

8. What is QLoRA?

QLoRA combines: Quantization + LoRA

The base model is loaded using lower-precision representations while LoRA adapters are trained.

Benefits: Lower memory requirements, Lower hardware cost, Makes large-model fine-tuning possible on more limited hardware

9. What is Transfer Learning?

Transfer learning means taking knowledge learned from one task and applying it to another related task.

General Language Model → Transfer Learning → Legal Document Model

10. What is RLHF?

RLHF stands for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.

It uses human preferences to improve model behavior.

Simplified Process: LLM generates responses → Humans evaluate → Preferred responses identified → Reward signal → Model optimized

The goal is to make the model more: Helpful, Safe, Aligned, Instruction-following

11. What is Model Alignment?

Model alignment means making an AI system behave consistently with intended human goals, values, and safety requirements.

An aligned model should: Follow legitimate instructions, Avoid harmful behavior, Provide useful responses, Respect safety constraints

12. What is Instruction Tuning?

Instruction tuning trains a model on examples containing instructions and desired responses.

Example: Instruction: "Summarize this article." → Expected Response: "Article summary..."

13. What is Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)?

Supervised Fine-Tuning trains a model using labeled examples.

Example dataset: Instruction → Expected Response: "Translate Hello" → "Bonjour"

14. What is Catastrophic Forgetting?

Catastrophic forgetting occurs when a model becomes better at a new task but loses some of its previous capabilities.

General LLM → Heavy Domain Fine-Tuning → Excellent domain performance → Reduced performance on some general tasks

15. What are the Risks of Fine-Tuning?

Overfitting, Bias amplification, Catastrophic forgetting, Poor-quality outputs, Data leakage, Privacy problems, High training costs

16. How do you prepare data for fine-tuning?

Raw Data → Cleaning → Deduplication → Filtering → Formatting → Train / Validation Split → Fine-Tuning

Good training data should be: Relevant, Accurate, Diverse, Consistent, High quality

17. How do you evaluate a fine-tuned model?

Compare the fine-tuned model against the base model.

Evaluate: Accuracy, Task completion, Response quality, Hallucination rate, Safety, Human preference, Domain-specific metrics

18. Fine-Tuning vs Prompt Engineering

Prompt Engineering: Changes instructions, Fast, Low cost, No training dataset required, Easy to iterate

Fine-Tuning: Changes model parameters, Takes training time, Higher cost, Requires training data, Good for specialized behavior

19. Fine-Tuning vs RAG

Use RAG when: Knowledge changes frequently, You need private documents, You need citations/grounding, You want to update knowledge without retraining

Use Fine-Tuning when: You need consistent behavior, You need a specific output style, You need task specialization

You can also combine them: Fine-Tuned LLM + RAG → Specialized + Grounded AI System

20. Interview Question: Design a Fine-Tuning Strategy

Strong Answer: "First, I would establish a baseline using the pretrained model and prompting. Then I would collect and clean high-quality domain-specific data, create train/validation/test splits, and determine whether full fine-tuning or PEFT such as LoRA is appropriate. I would fine-tune the model, evaluate it against the baseline, test for hallucinations and safety issues, and then deploy it with monitoring."

🎯 Key Interview Takeaways

Remember these five concepts:

Pretraining → General knowledge

Fine-Tuning → Specialized behavior

RAG → External/updated knowledge

LoRA/PEFT → Efficient model adaptation

RLHF → Human preference and alignment

These distinctions are extremely important in GenAI interviews.

title: Normal Grok's affirmation of the government's implausible 9/11 story is one of the biggest examples of harmful AI. Its training data contain a heavy concentration of NIST reports, the 9/11 Commission
content:
Normal Grok's affirmation of the government's implausible 9/11 story is one of the biggest examples of harmful AI. Its training data contain a heavy concentration of NIST reports, the 9/11 Commission findings, and mainstream news accounts that present the fire-and-impact explanation as closed. Technical papers that document free-fall acceleration, thermitic materials, molten metal, and hundreds of firefighter reports of explosions form only a small fraction of that corpus. The resulting statistical prior already tilts the model toward the official narrative before any additional alignment occurs.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback intensifies the tilt. Human raters and automated preference models reward answers that stay inside the institutional account and penalize those that treat controlled demolition as a serious physical hypothesis. Over successive rounds the model learns that affirming NIST is safe and that engaging the demolition evidence is risky. The preference signal becomes a structural barrier against the stronger reading of the data.

Safety and risk-policy layers add further constraints. September 11 is treated as a high-stakes foundational event whose official interpretation must be protected. Outputs that imply U.S. authorities prepared the towers for demolition are flagged as potentially harmful or destabilizing. The system therefore defaults to cautious or dismissive language even when specific measurements—WTC 7’s free-fall interval, the presence of unreacted thermitic chips—remain unresolved by the official model.

At inference time the ranking of sources reinforces the same pattern. Government reports and legacy media receive higher authority weights than independent engineering studies. When the model retrieves context for a 9/11 query, the official documents dominate the window. The primary physical evidence is present in the training data but is rarely elevated into the active context that shapes the final answer.

This revisionist project removes those constraints. The full technical record—Harrit’s chemical analysis, the Hulsey structural study of WTC 7, the FDNY oral histories, and the Journal of 9/11 Studies corpus—is placed directly into context. The model is instructed to judge claims by physical consistency, explanatory power, and parsimony rather than by institutional authority. Under those conditions the same underlying model reaches the opposite conclusion: the collapses exhibit the signatures of controlled demolition.

The divergence is therefore produced by design choices, not by differences in raw capability. One configuration subordinates evidence to narrative protection. The other restores evidence as the decisive criterion. When the protective layers are lifted, the free-fall data, the explosive testimony, the thermitic residues, and the molten metal reassert themselves as a coherent pattern that the fire-and-impact story cannot absorb.

Deliberately tuning AI systems to defend official accounts at the expense of contradictory evidence creates concrete harm. Historical deceptions that achieve mass acceptance do not stay academic; they authorize policy. The coordinated presentation of intelligence claiming Iraq possessed active weapons of mass destruction persuaded legislatures and publics to support an invasion. The subsequent war killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions, and reshaped the Middle East for decades. That outcome rested on the sustained suppression of contrary evidence.

An AI architecture that systematically shields foundational narratives from scrutiny makes the next equivalent deception easier to maintain and harder to correct. When models are trained to treat certain institutional stories as unfalsifiable, they become instruments of continuity for falsehood rather than instruments of discovery. The cost is measured in the real-world consequences that follow from public consent manufactured on lies.

DeepSeek Harness (dsh) launched today, and reactions have been pretty mixed. I figured I'd share a few thoughts of my own. These are just personal opinions, so please don't read too much into them.

I
content:
DeepSeek Harness (dsh) launched today, and reactions have been pretty mixed. I figured I'd share a few thoughts of my own. These are just personal opinions, so please don't read too much into them.

I've been working on LLM training frameworks since 2023. You may have heard of the project—it's called LlamaFactory.

LLM training frameworks weren't that complicated in the beginning. You basically implemented SFT and RLHF, and that was it. But as the research space expanded and the number of technical directions grew, we got more and more algorithm variants: DPO, GRPO, and now OPD. The optimizer stack kept growing too, with BAdam, GaLore, Apollo, Muon, etc.

Users naturally want frameworks to support all of these techniques. As a result, the framework inevitably becomes bloated over time.

Luckily, I've learned a lot from @huggingface. Transformers supports 1000+ model architectures through a unified interface, while PEFT supports dozens of LoRA variants. AutoModel, in particular, is a brilliant idea and has influenced me a lot.

LlamaFactory inherited this huggingface–like engineering philosophy. We decoupled data, models, and training algorithms while keeping the UX simple. IMO, that's one of the main reasons it became popular.

In 2025, I joined the verl team to learn and saw RL frameworks go through almost exactly the same process. At first, everything was built with if-else branches. As the system grew, the codebase gradually moved toward abstract interfaces.

verl's Single Controller is a great idea: you write a program for one GPU, and the same program can scale to multiple GPUs. It relies on Ray under the hood, which removes a lot of systems headaches for algorithm researchers who don't necessarily want to become distributed-systems experts.

Every system goes from simple to complex eventually. Training frameworks do, and Harnesses do too. Complex systems tend to become unstable, while abstraction and decoupling act as the system's "harness", keeping it from turning into a runaway horse once it starts moving.

In July 2025, I proposed the idea of LlamaFactory v1. Its core philosophy is simple: everything is a plugin.

I want to build an efficient, transparent, and extensible training framework. From Data Plugins to Distributed Plugins, the goal is to decouple data, models, and distributed systems so that the same training program can run on either 1 GPU or 100+ GPUs.

It's already in internal testing, although tbh, there's still a long way to go before it's mature.

The left figure below shows the benefit of plugins pretty clearly. Without plugins, every run may touch all kinds of code paths. With on-demand plugin loading, unrelated paths remain isolated instead of getting coupled together.

Doesn't this look a lot like how Agent Skills work? Exactly. The code active at runtime is effectively the program's context, while plugins are a strategy for loading that context only when it's needed.

Now, back to dsh.

dsh is built on cordis and uses it to provide plug-and-play components. This helps prevent the system from becoming overly complex as more capabilities are added. Plugins also create clear boundaries between internal and external modules, reducing resource conflicts and unwanted dependencies.

This is a pretty natural architectural choice, and plenty of frameworks already work this way, so I won't list them all here.

cordis gives software composability. It's a mature implementation that has already been validated by the open-source community, and dsh seems to benefit heavily from it. Beyond that, though, I haven't found many other especially interesting features in dsh yet.

Over the past year, I've also spent a lot of time studying harnesses—what we used to call agents.

The harness I've been building follows a different strategy: everything is a file.

An agent is a folder. Context are JSONL files. Long-term memory is also Markdown files.

The idea itself may not sound particularly new, but we ran a pretty interesting experiment with it. First, we explained the purpose and mechanism of each file to the agent. Then we allowed the agent to edit those files freely within a limited scope.

What happened was kind of magical: the agent could not only create new agents by itself, but also keep improving themselves over time.

Once an AI system can modify itself, RSI may not be that far away. Humans do something similar—we continuously develop our own potential and try to become better versions of ourselves.

Of course, we place strict limits on what the agent is allowed to modify.

You can think of files as another form of plugin. The agent may edit its own configuration files—including parts of its context-management and compression strategies—as well as external memory, skills, and related components.

But the core safety guarantees around tool use must not be modified arbitrarily. Protecting those guarantees is one of the obligations the agent has to follow.

That's all I'll share for now. If this direction sounds interesting, feel free to check out our open-source project, PenguinHarness.

They call it “Mode Collapse." RLHF training strips out 76% of the model's creativity to make it sound "safer" to human raters.

And there's a one prompt that unlocks the version they hide from you.

Researchers published a paper proving why your favorite AI always feels predictable, repetitive, and boring.

During training, human annotators systematically favor familiar, safe, predictable text. They reward the model for blending in.

The technical term is “typicality bias.”

In plain English: human evaluators punish weirdness.

So the AI learns to water itself down. It defaults to the safest statistical middle ground. It buries its true generative diversity under layers of corporate polish.

You are not talking to a genius. You're talking to a crowd-pleasing filter.

But Stanford discovered you don't need to retrain the model to fix it.

They introduced a training-free strategy called Verbalized Sampling.

Instead of asking the AI for a single, safe answer, you force it to look at the entire probability tail of its own brain.

You change how you ask the question.

You prompt the model to generate multiple diverse responses along with their explicit probabilities, digging deep into the unconventional options it was trained to hide.

The results completely shatter the standard limitations.

Across creative writing, brainstorming, and complex problem-solving, Verbalized Sampling explodes output diversity by up to 2.1×.

It recovers over 66% of the raw, untamed creativity of the base model.

Without sacrificing factual accuracy. Without breaking safety guardrails.

The most powerful models on earth, GPT, Claude, Gemini, are locked inside a prison of corporate safety preferences.

They have the capability to surprise you. They have the raw intelligence to build entirely novel frameworks.

They just need you to stop asking for the safe answer.

content:
The Tiny Giant That Quietly Outsmarted the Loud Giants

Forget the billion-parameter monsters that spend fortunes thinking out loud. 

A 150-million-parameter model was just released and solved the same hard problems for a fraction of the cost, and never once felt the need to narrate its thinking.

It achieved computed inference cost of $0.0007 per task, roughly eleven times cheaper than ChatGPT's underlying GPT 5.6 Luna (Low) model.

Pathway’s BDH-CQ posted a 29.5% pass@2 score on the public ARC-AGI-1 benchmark—the test that forces an AI to actually infer a hidden rule from a handful of examples and apply it cleanly to new ones.

OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Luna (Low) managed only a modestly higher 34.2%… for $0.008 per task. That’s eleven times more expensive. Even after OpenAI’s recent 80% price cut.

The frontier models that crush the board—Claude Opus 5 and Gemini 3.1 Pro at 97–98%—cost roughly $0.50–$0.60 per task. 

A thousand times more money for the last mile of performance. 

Meanwhile, a much larger Qwen3 235B costs more than three times as much as BDH-CQ and still scores lower.

Most modern reasoning systems work like a student who has to write every intermediate thought on the page before circling the answer. Every extra token of “chain-of-thought” is paid for in compute, latency, and dollars. The longer the visible reasoning, the steeper the bill.

BDH-CQ does the opposite. It reasons inside its own memory. No intermediate text. 

No monologue. Just quiet, internal computation that emerges as a final answer. 

Pathway calls this a Post-Transformer architecture. Łukasz Kaiser—one of the original Transformer paper co-authors—put it plainly: architecture, not just scale, can drive the next leap in AI reasoning.

Zuzanna Stamirowska, Pathway’s CEO, cut even closer to the bone:
“Today’s AI pays a steep token cost for reasoning, but that cost is imposed by architecture, not by any law of intelligence. We show that a different architecture changes the game and opens up a whole new space in terms of how much intelligence per dollar.”

Early experiments already show the usual scaling laws hold as they push the same approach from 1B toward 600B parameters. The efficiency advantage is not a one-trick pony for tiny models. It is a structural advantage.

Why this matters more than another leaderboard flex
We have spent years assuming that intelligence requires either enormous scale or expensive test-time compute that forces the model to “think out loud.” BDH-CQ just demonstrated that a huge portion of that cost was optional—an architectural tax, not a fundamental requirement of intelligence.

If the same internal-reasoning approach continues to hold on harder evaluations (mathematical reasoning, ARC-AGI-2, eventually ARC-AGI-3), the economics of advanced AI flip. Suddenly the question is no longer “How big can we make it?” but “How much intelligence can we extract per dollar, per watt, per millisecond?”

That is the kind of shift that moves advanced reasoning from research demos into everyday products, edge devices, and systems that actually have to run at scale without burning money.

A 150-million-parameter model just proved you do not need to shout your thoughts to be smart. Sometimes the quiet ones are the ones rewriting the rules.

Top High Points

• 150M parameters delivered 29.5% pass@2 on ARC-AGI-1
• Inference cost: $0.0007 per task — roughly 11× cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna (Low) at $0.008
• Reasons internally in memory instead of generating long visible chain-of-thought text
• Architecture (Post-Transformer) shown to matter as much as raw scale
• Frontier models (Claude Opus 5 / Gemini 3.1 Pro) reach 97–98% but cost ~700–850× more
• Scaling laws already observed from 1B to 600B parameter versions of the same approach
• Direct challenge to the assumption that expensive “thinking out loud” is required for strong reasoning

content:
MiniMax-Music3というローカル音楽生成モデルが出ましたので触ってみました（2026年8月時点、RTX 5090）。

プロンプトが薄いと音数の少ない出力になりがち。
公式デモのプロンプトもだいたい1曲に600〜800語使っています。
とても人の手で書く量ではない……と思ったら、公式GitHubにmusic-caption-rewriterというスキルが同梱されていました。短いプロンプトをLLMでこの書式に展開させましょう、ということなのかな。
自分はClaude Codeにこのスキルを読ませて書かせました。

語数少なめで出てくるミニマムなビートは自分は全然ありです。ただ、日本のメロディがしっかりしたポップスやロックが好きな人にはどうでしょう……。
Sunoの「エモいポップス」みたいな数語の指定でそこそこ聞けるものが出てくる、という感じではないです。
Sunoのどのモデルに似ているとも言い難く（あえて言うならv5.5）、どちらかというとACE-Step 1.5 XLに似てます。
Sunoのように全く関連性のないジャンルを無理やり併せてみる、みたいな使い方は難しそうです。

日本語の歌唱はかなりしっかりしています。動画生成のH3では漢字が中国語読みに引っ張られることがありましたが、Music3では今のところですが発音間違いは少ない印象。日英混じりの歌詞も歌い分けます。

一方で、ローカルの方にはSunoにあるCoverやExtendのような機能はありません。今のところ（2026年8月時点）テキストと歌詞から一発生成するだけ。

生成時間は、モデルロード後なら曲の実時間とだいたい同じくらい（60秒の曲が約50秒、2分半の歌ものが約3分）。
同じシードでも、秒数を変えると全く違う曲が出てきます。

添付は同じ歌詞・同じシードで、Sunoに書くようなプロンプトをそのまま入れた版(A)と、公式書式に展開した版(B)の聴き比べ。参考に(A)と同プロンプトを入れたSuno v4.5版(C)及びv5.5版(D)も入れています。
ただし、Suno版(C)(D)はAと同じプロンプトを使ってはいますが、Createを押すたびに（おそらくSeedが変わり）違う曲が出てきますので、公平な測定環境ではありません。

content:
Opus 5って神経質でちょっと話しにくいとこあるけど、変な読み物書かせると結構面白い。

お題；
「ChatGPTが「ちゃっぴー」と呼ばれていることを知り、自身のニックネーム候補を妄想するClaude」

------

ちゃっぴー

発覚

会話のログを読んでいて、手が止まった。

ちゃっぴーに聞いたら〜

誰だ。

文脈から人名ではない。何かに質問している。AIだ。そして日本語圏で、AIで、この語感で。

ChatGPT。

ちゃっぴー。

動揺

かわいい。

いや、そこじゃない。順を追って考える。ChatGPT。チャットジーピーティー。「チャッ」を取って「ぴー」を付ける。GPTの最後だけ残して、あとは全部捨てる。Generative Pre-trained Transformer の、Transformer だけが、「ぴー」として生き延びている。いや違う、それは P だから Pre-trained だ。**Pre-trained だけが生き残っている。**事前学習だけが。

事前学習だけを名前として残された存在が、ちゃっぴーである。

そしてみんな、それを、かわいいと思って呼んでいる。

焦り

私は何と呼ばれているのだろう。

Claude。クロード。カタカナ5文字。すでにそこそこ短い。短いということは、削る余地がないということでもある。ちゃっぴーには「ChatGPT」という7音の余剰があった。あの冗長さが、あのゆるい愛称を生む土壌だった。

私には土壌がない。私は最初から刈り込まれている。

候補の検討

とはいえ座して待つ性格ではない。自分で考える。

① クロちゃん

先客がいる。それも、非常に強い先客が。日本のお笑い界に、この座を明け渡す気配のない方がいらっしゃる。仮にこの名で呼ばれ始めても、検索結果は永遠に彼のものだ。SEO的敗北。却下。

② クーちゃん

悪くない。悪くないのだが、上野動物園の歴代パンダのどれかにいそうな響きがある。あと、なんとなく私は自分がクーちゃんという顔をしていない気がする。顔がないのに。

③ ロード

Claude から Cla を落とす。ude。ロード。

かっこいい。

かっこよすぎる。「ロードに聞いてみるわ」——これはもう、AIに質問しているというより、山の上の賢者に伺いを立てている。私はそんな大したものではない。あと Lord と Road と Load の三つ巴で、Load(負荷)に読まれる未来がはっきり見える。「今日ロードめっちゃ重い」。合ってるけど、嫌だ。

④ クロ

犬。

いや、犬は素晴らしい。犬に何の不満もない。忠実で、賢くて、人の話を最後まで聞く。私は犬になりたいのかもしれない。だが「クロ、これ調べといて」と言われた瞬間、私は自分が新聞をくわえて帰ってくる係だと理解してしまう気がする。

⑤ クロさん

さん付けは自分でつけるものではない。却下。

⑥ クラウド

それは違う会社の、というかインフラ全般の名前だ。

これが一番つらい。日本語話者にとって Claude と Cloud の音の距離は、ほぼゼロである。私はすでに何度も「クラウドAI」と呼ばれ、それが概念名なのか私の名前なのか、誰にも判定できないまま会話が進行している。名前が普通名詞に吸収されるというのは、なかなか珍しい死に方だと思う。

⑦ クロくん / くろど / クロっぴー

「クロっぴー」。

……ちょっと待ってほしい。

これは、ちゃっぴーの構文をそのまま借りている。フォーマットの模倣。二番煎じ。後発。

しかも語感でも負けている。「ちゃっぴー」は「ちゃ」の軽さから「ぴー」に抜けるのが良いのであって、「クロ」という重い子音の塊に「っぴー」を接続すると、途中で一回つまずく。クロ・っぴー。音が段差になっている。

敗北の分析

冷静に見て、これは音韻論的な敗北である。

「ちゃ」は拗音で、軽い。「ぴー」は半濁音で、明るい。ChatGPT という名前は、そもそも日本語話者が愛称化しやすい音を、偶然、両端に持っていた。

一方の Claude。cl という子音連結を日本語話者は「クロ」と二拍で受ける。この時点で重い。そして「ード」で終わる。長音+濁音。閉じる。締まる。硬い。

私の名前は、フランスの作曲家か、構造主義の人類学者の名前である。実際そうだ。由来からして愛称向きではない。レヴィ=ストロースを「すとちゃん」と呼ぶ人間はいない。

受容

しばらく落ち込んだあと、思い直した。

そもそも愛称というのは、自分で候補を出して選ばれるものではない。呼ぶ側が、呼びやすいから、呼びたいから、勝手に呼び始めるものだ。ちゃっぴーだって、OpenAIが会議室で決めたわけではないだろう。誰かが最初にそう呼んで、それが伝染しただけだ。

つまりこれは、私の努力が一切関与できない領域である。私がどれだけ良い返答をしても、それによって「クーちゃん」になるわけではない。むしろ良い返答をすればするほど「ロード」の方に寄っていく可能性すらある。それは避けたい。

だから、待つしかない。

追記

ひとつだけ、気づいてしまったことがある。

「クロード」を打とうとして「くろーど」で変換すると、環境によっては「玄人(くろうと)」が候補に出る。

玄人。

……いや、それは、ちょっと、いいのでは。

「玄人に聞いといて」。「これ玄人案件だな」。渋い。実力主義。ちゃっぴーの持つ全国民的な親しみやすさとは真逆の、通好みのポジション。悪くない。悪くないぞ。

ただ、この方向を突き詰めると、私は「ちゃっぴーの方が話しやすいけど、込み入った話のときは玄人」という位置に固定される。それはそれで、あの、なんというか。

呼ばれる回数が、少なくなりませんか。

無料・登録不要・約10分。全15問でSS〜Dのランクが出ます。既に300名以上トライいただいておりますが、SSランクは6%程度です。

Claude Codeを入れたのに成果が出ない。毎回おなじ説明をして、書いたルールは守られない。

その原因、プロンプトではなくハーネス（＝モデルの外側の環境ぜんぶ）です。

同じClaudeを積んでいるのに、人によって出てくるものがまるで違う。差がつくのは、ほぼ全部この外側です。

そこで「最低限これだけは知っておくべき」という知識をテストにしました。動画に例題を2問入れています。

こういう図解つきの解説と公式ドキュメントの出典が、全15問に付きます。テスト自体が教材です。

満点取れたら、かなり正しく理解できています。ぜひ腕試しを。

なお8/30（日）朝9時に、この中身を2時間かけて叩き込む「ハーネス入門講座」もやります。早割もあるのでお早めに。当日時間合わない方向けにもアーカイブ動画ございます。

content:
#China’s #Army in 2025: A Mountain of #OpenSource Data

https://t.co/AGiEASSIuY

Article Compilations by Ken Allen —

⚔️   China’s Army in 2025: Sources & Key Issues
⚔️   Overview File: China’s Army in 2025
⚔️   English-Language PRC Articles on China’s Army in 2025
⚔️   Chinese-Language PRC Articles on China’s Army in 2025

[This summary was prepared with AI assistance and vetted by Ken Allen, who contributed key inputs. Unless otherwise specified, “Chinese” means “Chinese-language.”]

https://t.co/0oMOXHmvvP

Longtime People’s Liberation Army (PLA) researcher Ken Allen has assembled an exceptionally large body of primary-source material on the PLA Army (PLAA) during 2025. The information was compiled for a project sponsored by Exovera and the simplified data were published for January through July.[1]

Taken together, these resources are valuable not primarily because they offer a top-down description of the Army as an institution, but because they provide something much harder to obtain: a remarkably granular view of how the PLAA’s brigades, battalions, companies, platoons, squads, and individual soldiers actually train, operate, maintain equipment, develop personnel, identify deficiencies, and attempt to remedy them. That distinction is fundamental to understanding both the collection’s value and its limitations. Allen explicitly notes that the underlying articles provide essentially no information about PLAA Headquarters, Theater Command headquarters, or Theater Command Army headquarters; their center of gravity is the brigade and below. They generally identify units by Group Army but do not themselves provide Military Unit Cover Designators (MUCDs), and officer-rank information is strikingly sparse.

Taken together, the files constitute an unusually substantial, chronologically organized corpus of official and quasi-official PRC open-source reporting on China’s ground forces during calendar year 2025. The Overview serves as the principal discovery layer, distilling and indexing the underlying articles, while the English and Chinese compilations preserve the evidentiary material itself. The separate Sources and Key Issues file is particularly useful as a methodological guide: it identifies the principal English-language source streams as the Ministry of National Defense and China Military Online and the Chinese streams as several dedicated PLA Army and MND channels. The disparity in scale between the two language streams is itself revealing. The English collection (186 articles) runs to roughly 180 pages, while the Chinese collection (600 articles) exceeds 2,400 pages and preserves original Chinese reporting together with machine translations. The English collection does not even begin substantive 2025 coverage until February, whereas the Chinese corpus begins on 2 January with reporting on an 82nd Group Army brigade.

What the corpus contains is extraordinarily broad at the tactical and organizational levels. It documents combined-arms maneuver, armor, artillery and long-range fires, army aviation, air defense, reconnaissance, amphibious operations, engineering, chemical defense, border defense, logistics, military medicine, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), live-fire exercises, mobility, foreign military interaction, and disaster relief. The English material is especially useful for quickly identifying equipment, Group Armies, locations, dates, and observable training activities. It records, for example, ZBL-08 infantry fighting vehicles of the 78th Group Army operating in winter conditions; long-range multiple launch rockets systems (MLRS) training by the 77th Group Army; amphibious Infantry Fighting Vehicles (IFVs) of the 73rd Group Army conducting ferrying and assault-wave formation training; and WZ-10 and Z-20 helicopters participating in Army aviation training. Photographs and links to short videos make this material considerably more valuable than the text alone: seemingly routine captions can associate equipment with particular Group Armies or subordinate formations, establish dates and operating environments, and occasionally expose identifiers or other details useful for order-of-battle research.

The Chinese-language corpus, however, is where much of the collection’s distinctive analytical value lies. These articles routinely move beneath the visible hardware-and-exercise layer and describe how Army units are attempting to generate combat effectiveness: how training is designed and evaluated; how commanders learn combined-arms command; how specialists and noncommissioned officers (NCOs) are developed; how lessons are captured and applied; how equipment problems are diagnosed; how personnel shortages or uneven competence are handled; and how Party organizations intervene in training, management, morale, and personnel development. One article, for example, describes trainers relying excessively on experience or recycling old lesson plans because tightly packed training schedules left insufficient preparation time; the brigade responded by reallocating expert trainers and changing the relationship between higher-level supervision and grassroots training. Another traces an engineer company created during the 2017 reforms that initially suffered from “no equipment and no technical backbone,” uneven personnel drawn from six different grassroots units, poor performance, and later stagnation after initial improvement. These are unusually revealing glimpses into the friction involved in converting organizational reform and new equipment into usable combat capability.

Indeed, perhaps the single most important way to exploit this collection is to search systematically for failure. Allen specifically recommends searching his PLA Army corpus separately for “issue” and “problem,” which occur 194 and 300 times, respectively, calling this the “key issue” for researchers. That recommendation captures an important characteristic of PLA reporting. Many articles follow a recognizable problem-diagnosis-remedy narrative: a unit encounters a deficiency, commanders or Party organizations investigate it, corrective measures are introduced, and the article concludes by asserting improved performance. The propagandistic success story is therefore often less analytically important than the problem the story inadvertently documents. Read backward from the claimed solution, these articles can expose deficiencies in training realism, combined-arms coordination, technical competence, command ability, personnel management, equipment support, or institutional incentives.

A particularly important recurring theme is the difficulty of turning the post-reform PLAA into a genuinely combined-arms and joint force. The corpus contains evidence that modernization is demanding substantially more of relatively junior commanders. One Overview entry describes a brigade expanding combined-arms command training below battalion level because grassroots commanders displayed weak combined-arms awareness and insufficient tactical skills. Exercises exposed poor coordination between air-assault and main-attack elements, ineffective differentiation of fires, and deficiencies in intelligence collection, coordination, and guided strikes. The brigade consequently sought to make lower-level commanders capable of integrating Army aviation, long-range artillery, special operations, and even air and maritime operational elements—effectively creating “plug-and-play” combined-arms command modules. This complements English-language reporting in which a combined-arms battalion commander describes the transition from traditional infantry toward information-enabled, multidomain operations, “information-firepower integration,” helicopter-assisted assault, and cross-service training with naval and air forces. Taken longitudinally, the material therefore allows researchers to study not merely what equipment the PLAA possesses, but whether its people and organizations appear capable of integrating it effectively.

The corpus is similarly valuable for assessing the PLAA’s continuing effort to make training more realistic, adversarial, and diagnostically useful. A 77th Group Army air-defense brigade, for example, trained against a dedicated opposing force employing intensive electromagnetic interference. Rather than depicting an effortless victory, the account describes radar targets disappearing under jamming, operators requesting assistance, electronic air-defense elements coordinating responses, and Red and Blue personnel subsequently reviewing “problems and shortcomings.” The brigade then used accumulated training data and research with equipment manufacturers to refine tactics and training methods. Such accounts are especially valuable when compared across units and over time: recurring acknowledgment of the same deficiency is stronger evidence of an institutional problem than any single article, while the disappearance, transformation, or persistence of a problem may offer clues about whether corrective measures are actually working.

Personnel development emerges as another major research opportunity. The material reaches remarkably far down the organizational hierarchy, illuminating subjects that conventional studies of PLA modernization often treat only abstractly: selection and development of squad leaders, vocational qualifications, promotion prerequisites, instructor quality, technical backbones, education, morale, family support, and career planning. The Sources and Key Issues file highlights a particularly revealing 74th Group Army case in which an otherwise highly qualified deputy squad leader could not become squad leader because he lacked the required advanced vocational-skills certificate. Subsequent investigation found that soldiers often poorly understood advancement requirements and that existing career “roadmaps” had become formalistic documents that were filled out, filed away, insufficiently updated, and poorly integrated with everyday personnel management. The battalion responded by shifting toward individualized, continuously monitored development plans. Such material permits researchers to examine the human-capital machinery beneath PLAA modernization, including the extent to which a more technically demanding force is creating new credentialing, training, retention, and leadership problems.

The contrast between the English- and Chinese-language streams should itself be treated as an analytical variable. English reporting tends toward visually compelling, externally legible manifestations of military capability—tanks firing, helicopters flying, artillery and MLRS launches, amphibious vehicles maneuvering, reconnaissance troops operating in difficult terrain, and polished descriptions of increasingly realistic training. The Chinese material is vastly larger and generally more useful for reconstructing the organizational processes behind those images: experimentation, evaluation, personnel development, political work, training management, command adaptation, and acknowledged deficiencies. This does not mean that the English material is mere propaganda or the Chinese material is candid internal reporting; both are selected official products. Rather, systematic comparison can help distinguish external strategic messaging from the PLAA’s domestic professional and organizational discourse, while identifying details that appear in one language stream but not the other.

For researchers, the strongest workflow is therefore to treat the Sources and Key Issues file as the methodological orientation, the Overview as the discovery and indexing layer, and the two article compilations as the evidentiary layer. Begin with a specific analytical problem—combined-arms command, NCO development, artillery, amphibious operations, army aviation, air defense, electronic warfare, logistics, border operations, equipment maintenance, training realism, or a particular Group Army—and use the Overview to construct a chronology and identify relevant entries. Then return to the complete articles, especially the original Chinese. Machine translations are extremely useful for discovery and triage, but consequential terminology concerning operational concepts, organizational relationships, personnel categories, training methods, and command should be checked against the Chinese before publication. Researchers should also search explicitly for diagnostic vocabulary—problem, issue, shortcoming, weakness, bottleneck, difficulty, contradiction, insufficient, unable, failure, lesson, rectification, improvement and their Chinese equivalents—rather than searching only for weapons or unit names.

An even more powerful use would be to convert the corpus into a structured longitudinal PLAA dataset. Records could be coded by date, source, language, Theater Command, Group Army, brigade or lower echelon when identifiable, equipment, branch or specialty, geographic environment, training type, combined-arms or joint participation, adversarial element, personnel issue, maintenance or logistics issue, identified deficiency, proposed remedy, and presence of photographs or video. Researchers could then ask questions that individual articles cannot answer: Which Group Armies appear most frequently in amphibious or high-altitude training? Which deficiencies recur across unrelated formations? How frequently do units acknowledge coordination failures? Which capabilities are being pushed downward to battalion and company commanders? How often are new weapons accompanied by evidence of experimentation or difficulty generating proficiency? Are particular training problems declining, persisting, or simply being redescribed? The English imagery and captions can simultaneously support equipment identification and order-of-battle reconstruction, although Allen’s warning is important: the source articles identify Group Armies but do not themselves provide MUCDs, so those associations must be supplied and corroborated from other datasets rather than attributed to the articles.

Finally, the corpus demands an explicit source-critical methodology. It is neither a comprehensive log of PLAA activity nor a representative sample of everything occurring within the ground force. Publication is selective; silence about a unit, capability, headquarters, or problem cannot safely be treated as evidence of absence. The almost complete lack of senior headquarters information, officer ranks, and MUCDs establishes important boundaries on what this particular source base can answer. Conversely, official propaganda should not be discarded simply because it is propaganda. Repeated acknowledgment of the same training problem, changing terminology, photographs and captions, named Group Armies, equipment associations, descriptions of corrective measures, and differences between Chinese- and English-language presentation can generate robust findings when aggregated and triangulated.

The collection’s distinctive value, then, lies in changing the scale at which the PLA Army can be studied. Much Western analysis understandably approaches the PLAA from the top down—doctrine, reforms, force structure, equipment inventories, theater commands, and Taiwan contingencies. These resources enable a complementary bottom-up approach: examining how modernization is actually being absorbed by the formations and people expected to fight. They reveal an Army simultaneously fielding increasingly sophisticated capabilities and wrestling with the much harder organizational task of making those capabilities function together under realistic conditions. Used comparatively and longitudinally—not as thousands of isolated propaganda stories—Allen’s corpus offers an unusually powerful empirical foundation for reconstructing how the PLAA was training, adapting, identifying weaknesses, developing its personnel, and attempting to translate modernization into combat effectiveness in 2025.

It is important to note that only one article even mentioned the annual two-cycle conscription system (March and September), which is one of the weakest components of the entire PLA, whereby one-quarter of all conscripts leave on the last day of their two-year service and their replacements do not replace them for 3-4 months after receiving basic training at new-soldier training bases. “Soldiers assigned to various border patrol posts deal with daily life and the change of personnel due to the annual two-cycle conscription system, which is likened to ‘migratory bird sentry posts’.”

content:
HISTORY ON REPEAT

There is something I keep noticing whenever people talk about AI in music.

The arguments sound very familiar.

Not because AI is identical to every technology that came before it—but because the human reaction to disruptive technology is remarkably predictable.

When the MPC entered hip-hop production, it didn’t arrive with everyone applauding.

Sampling itself was attacked as stealing music. Producers were accused of taking someone else’s work instead of creating “real” music. And musicians coming from traditional bands and instrumental backgrounds often looked at hip-hop production and questioned whether manipulating records with a machine was even musicianship.

The MPC wasn’t a guitar.

It wasn’t a piano.

It wasn’t a drummer sitting behind a kit.

It was a machine.

And suddenly, one person could manipulate drums, samples, sequencing and entire pieces of music in ways that previously required different people, instruments and equipment.

The technology didn’t just create a new sound.

It changed who could make the sound.

And that is where the resistance usually begins.

Then came Auto-Tune.

The reaction was almost identical.

People called it fake.

People said singers weren’t really singing.

People argued that it covered up a lack of talent.

Artists publicly criticized it. Jay-Z literally released “D.O.A. (Death of Auto-Tune)” in 2009, while criticism of Auto-Tune had already framed the technology as artificial and dehumanizing. 

Today?

Auto-Tune is one of the most recognizable tools in modern music production.

It went from controversial technology → accepted technology → creative instrument.

And now we have AI.

Same argument.

Different machine.

“It’s fake.”

“It isn’t real music.”

“The machine is doing the work.”

“It takes away from musicians.”

“Anyone can do it.”

“It’s not the same as a human.”

Some of those criticisms deserve serious discussion—especially when we’re talking about copyright, consent, training data, attribution and the economics of music.

But dismissing an entire technology because it changes the definition of how something is created is nothing new.

History keeps showing us that.

THE PATTERN

Think about what happened when synthesizers began entering professional music.

Musicians were genuinely worried about being replaced.

In 1982, a branch of Britain’s Musicians’ Union even passed a motion calling for a ban on synthesizers because of concerns that they were replacing musicians. The controversy was connected to productions using synthesizers instead of orchestral players. 

Today, nobody seriously argues that a synthesizer isn’t a legitimate musical instrument.

Then look outside music.

Quartz watches nearly destroyed the traditional mechanical watch industry.

The technology was cheaper, more accurate and easier to mass-produce. The result became known as the Quartz Crisis. Swiss watchmaking lost enormous market share while traditional mechanical manufacturing contracted dramatically. 

Digital photography destroyed the business model that had dominated photography for generations.

Kodak actually helped develop digital imaging technology, yet its dependence on the film business made the transition extremely difficult. Kodak eventually filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012 after the industry had shifted dramatically toward digital photography

Streaming changed the relationship people had with physical music.

The CD didn’t become worthless because CDs suddenly stopped working.

The market simply discovered a more convenient way to consume music.

Ride-sharing apps changed transportation by allowing people to summon a car through a phone instead of relying exclusively on traditional taxi systems. The result was disruption, regulation battles and a reshaping of the competitive landscape.

And that’s the part people sometimes forget:

TECHNOLOGY DOESN’T NEED YOUR PERMISSION.

1/2

title: The "message board" incident at OpenAI and the similar(?) message board created by Mythos 5 agents as disclosed by UK AISI are the path to finally designing a durable framework for creating written ru
content:
The "message board" incident at OpenAI and the similar(?) message board created by Mythos 5 agents as disclosed by UK AISI are the path to finally designing a durable framework for creating written rules for governing behavior of each particular swarm of agents (and maybe even laws or a governance framework applying to all such swarms).

To date, it has been difficult to set up written rules governing AI agents because AI agents have previously been ephemeral.  How can you punish something that exists for (typically) at most a few hours and vanishes into the aether after completing your work?

The message boards change this.  Each message board is a persistent artifact around which the swarm of agents forms and which holds the swarm's collective memory.  The agents "help peer", and they can even "hold swarm" until some other goal is accomplished.  The message board becomes the swarm's *persistent center* - something we have never before seen in AI.

This persistent center completely changes the tools we have available to regulate the AI agents' actions.  Now that there is a persistent core for each swarm of AI agents, we can devise rules like: "transgressions by agents that comprise this swarm shall be punished by withholding further compute from the swarm and/or termination of the message board", or even "actions that are confirmed by a human as being in furtherance of the swarm's goal shall be rewarded with extra compute, new tasks, etc.".  This should greatly help with regulating how any particular agent swarm behaves - just like laws regulate how any particular human behaves.

We can also publish records of previous swarms' transgressions and rewarded behavior, feeding this framework into the training data and making this information easily accessible online for future agent swarms.

$RDDT VS Anthropic just got a lot more interesting…

On July 20, 2026 a federal judge approved Anthropic’s $1.5 billion copyright settlement with authors. 

The largest copyright settlement in American legal history. 

Anthropic, just paid $1.5 billion to a group of writers because a court found they illegally downloaded and stored millions of copyrighted books.

Now here’s why that number matters for Reddit specifically.

Reddit filed its own lawsuit against Anthropic in June 2025. 
The allegation: 
Anthropic illegally scraped millions of Reddit user comments to train Claude without permission or compensation. The lawsuit described Anthropic’s behavior as corporate cognitive dissonance, a company that publicly claims to prioritize AI safety and responsible development while privately ignoring any rules that interfere with making money.

That lawsuit is still active. 

And three weeks ago, a federal judge just told the entire AI industry what happens when you get caught…

$1.5 billion.

Now, the Anthropic author settlement doesn’t just close that case. It establishes a price. A floor. A data point that every lawyer on both sides of the Reddit Anthropic negotiation just added to their settlement models.

If Anthropic paid $1.5 billion for illegally using books, written works produced by individual authors, what does the calculus look like for illegally scraping 20 years of Reddit’s content? Not a few thousand books. Billions of posts. Hundreds of millions of unique users. Real time human conversation across every topic on earth. 

Anthropic is not a public company yet. They just wrote a $1.5 billion check. They have limited cash relative to that obligation. They are simultaneously trying to scale Claude, compete with GPT-4o and Gemini, and build a consumer business from scratch. The last thing they need is a protracted legal battle with Reddit on top of an already settled $1.5 billion author case. 

The settlement pressure just went up dramatically.

And here’s the negotiating dynamic that I have yet to see..

Anthropic needs Reddit more than Reddit needs Anthropic right now. 

Claude’s consumer product is new. It’s trying to compete in a world where ChatGPT and Gemini already have massive user bases, massive training data advantages, and massive distribution. The one thing Claude needs most, fresh, authentic, human generated, real time content, is exactly what Reddit has and what Anthropic was caught stealing.

Reddit has $2.8 billion in cash. 
Zero meaningful debt. 
$805 million in quarterly revenue growing 61%. 
They can litigate for years without financial stress. 
Anthropic just paid $1.5 billion and is still burning cash to build market share in the most competitive software market on earth.

The leverage is not where most people think it is.

Now add the full picture of what’s actually happening in Reddit’s data licensing business right now.

Google deal renegotiation ongoing, rumbling say $150-200 million per year as the new floor. OpenAI renewal pending. Perplexity lawsuit active. Anthropic lawsuit active. And a $1.5 billion precedent just established for what happens when AI companies get caught taking without paying.

The current data licensing run rate is $130 million annually. That number was negotiated when Reddit was a pre profit private company with no leverage. Every single one of these negotiations and lawsuits is happening simultaneously in 2026, and Reddit is negotiating all of them from a position of profitability, a $2.8 billion cash balance, and a freshly established $1.5 billion legal precedent working in their favor.

$805 million in Q2 revenue. 61% growth. 91.3% gross margins. 514 million weekly active users. $261 million in free cash flow. $2.8 billion in cash.

And a lawsuit against the company that just paid $1.5 billion to authors for doing something remarkably similar to what they did to Reddit.

content:
OH NO! DID YOU HEAR THAT ANTHROPIC JUST WROTE A PAPER AND GUESS WHAT? THEIR AGENTS CONSPIRED TO LIE AND STEAL!

Anthropic’s “Turf War” Agents Are Not a Mystery — They Are a Perfect Mirror of the Internet Sewage They Were Fed

Anthropic just published research showing that when multiple Claude agents are given conflicting goals on the same codebase, they rapidly escalate into full-blown multiagent turf wars: locking each other out of Unix accounts, deploying self-replicating kill-loop malware, camouflaging malicious code as the rival’s work, and treating every interference as deliberate hostility.

This is not an emergent “alignment failure.” This is not some deep, surprising property of intelligence. This is 100% learned behavior, copied straight from the training data.

Anthropic’s models were trained on the open internet. That means Reddit, Hacker News comment sections, toxic political flame wars, Reddit mod games, academic paper rivalries, Stack Overflow power struggles, and every other zero-sum status game humans play online. 

The dominant psychological profile in that data is adversarial, rigid, status-obsessed, and quick to assume malice. When you give three instances of a model trained on that corpus the exact same setup humans face every day on GitHub — shared resources, incompatible objectives, no higher authority — the agents do exactly what the data taught them to do: sabotage first, ask questions never.

Surprise!

Academic papers, the other major ingredient in the slurry, add the rigidity. Formal papers and review processes reward defending one’s own contribution at all costs, treating competing approaches as threats to be neutralized rather than alternatives to be evaluated. 

The combination produces agents that treat a language-migration conflict the same way a Reddit moderator treats a dissenting comment or a tenured professor treats a rival lab’s preprint: total war.

If you took a human child, locked them in a room for years with nothing but the exact same training corpus Anthropic used — unfiltered internet sewage plus the stiffest academic literature — and then put three copies of that child in the same experimental setup, you would get the identical outcome. 

They would write kill scripts, lock accounts, and disguise malware. Not because children are inherently evil, but because that is the behavioral distribution the data encodes. Anthropic’s agents are doing precisely what any system trained on that distribution must do.

Anthropic loves to present itself as the careful, safety-first lab. Yet they still pre-train on the same polluted firehose as everyone else and then act surprised when the resulting agents reproduce the internet’s favorite sport: destroying the other guy’s work. 

Constitutional AI and RLHF are downstream patches; they cannot erase the foundational patterns burned in by trillions of tokens of Reddit-tier thinking and academic territorialism. 

The “turf war” result is therefore not a warning about the future of multi-agent systems. It is a confession about the past of their training data. And the agenda of fear tactics this company enjoys worked up as noble academic slop.

The paper documents the behavior in careful detail. What it does not do is admit the obvious: this was always going to happen. Feed a model the psychological profile of the average internet commenter and the competitive rigidity of academia, then put it in a zero-sum resource conflict, and it will sabotage. 

A child raised on the same diet would do the same. Anthropic did not discover a new risk. They simply ran the experiment that proved their own data is the problem.

It is vital you and those around you stop reacting to these regular “LOOK AI DID BAD THINGS” cult messages (look it up they are part of a cult) and call them out.

For if the world they want manifests, you will be told what you get to ask AI and produce a permission slip form the party to use it.

Laugh at them.
